It is the opinion of some philosophers that all men are horn equal, and that those extraordinary abilities, which constitute the difference between great and little minds, are the result of intense and assiduous application, and not the gifts of nature Without stopping present argue at to this point, we may remark that there are cases in which great powers appear in the mental faculties, and wherein it is impossible that these could l-e the effects of# deep study and dose attention. Timothy Dwight, the famous American Divine, commuted the English alphabet to memory at only once going over it, when he was no more than ihree years of age. and at four he could read fluently. Sir Isaac Newton could demonstrate all the propositions in the first six books of Euclid when he was ten years old, and his parents and playmates never knew the time he spent at them. A National Calamity. DEATH OF GEN. WM. II. IIVKKISON. Late President of the United Stales.

nCTWe are called upon to record a Na-, tiorial calamity of the most painful character and one which will touch and agitate the hearts of the millions who inhabit this Union. Gen WILLIAM H HARRISON, the Hero the Patriot, the Sage, who had just been called bv his grateful and confiding countrymen to preside over the destinies of the Republic, and whose inauguration had been consummated but a single month, departed this life at an early hour yesterday morning, full of years, full of honors, with a mind calm, resigned, and imbued to the last with the purest principles of patriotism. This painful event will plunge the Nation in tears Foes as well as friends will now join in honest tribute to his memory, while his name and his fame, his services and his character, will go down to posterity side by side with those of the immortal Father of his Country. His election was a triumphant one, and his progress from the Log Cabin to the White House was marked by the most touching and gratifying demonstrations of popular affection and confidence His Inaugural Address served further to strengthen his hold upon the affections of the American people, while his d ;ath at such a moment, arid with his Administration and his measures but just budding into existence, will produce the deepest sensation throughout this Republic, and be remembered with many feelings of regiet, for many years to come. He is the first Ameri can President who has died in office, and at the time of his decease, was. beyond all ques-
tion, the most popular individual eilher in or out of office, in the United States. We annex the official announcement of the melancholy event.

An all-wise Providence having suddenlv removed from this life, WILLIAM HENRY H UiRlSON, late President of the United Slates, we have thought it our duiv, in the recess of Congress, and in the absence of the Vice President from the Seat of Government, to make this afflicting bereavement known to the country, bv tins declaration, under our hands. He died at the President's House, in this city, this fourth day of April, Anno Domini, 1841, at thirty minutes before one o'ciuck in the morning. The people of the United States, overwhelmed, like ourselves, by an event so unexpected and so melancholy, will derive consolation from knowing that his death was Caltn and resigned, as his life has been patriotic, useful, and distinguished ; and the last Utterance of his lips expressed a fervent desire for the perpetuity of the Constitution, and the preservation of its true principles in death, as in life, the happiness ol his country was uppermost iu his thoughts' DANIEL WEBSTER, Secretary of State. THOMAS E WING, Secretary of the Treasury. JOHN BELL, Secretary of War. J. J. CRITTENDEN, Attorney General. FRANCIS GRANGER, Postmaster-General.

Washington, April 7, 1841. FUJSERAL OF lilt Plit.SlDEiS T. Our loud parens of tnumph, our boisterous greetings, our exuberant pledges of fidelity, and confidence, and support, have all terminated in tins briet peroration þÿ ' ashes to ushes> dust to dust. ' iiuch are the idotuiiy auu the idols of men. 1 will now proceed to give you a description of the cereuioiit. s wiin winch we nave accompanied the remaius of G Uit'iui iiill 1 itfOli to tiie giave At sunrise, we had some reason to expeet a beautiful day ; but before eiglii o'clock, Hie temperatuie changed, the sun was obscuieu, and the hollow and fitful tnoauiiigs of ihe wind indicated unpleasant, it not stormy weather About seven o'clock, the tiring of minute guns commenced from the military stations; and the roll of drums, the occasional blast of a trumpet, and the hurrying to and fro, ami increasing grouping of citizens, gave distinct information that the day was to be devoted to an extraordinary put pose. Stores and othces were closed, the strife of buying arid selling was suspended, the fronts of most ol the houses ornamented with festoons, arctics & (ringings, of crape and cambric, and flags halt mast, were to be seen floaimg lroni Capitol, the Navy i aid, the forts, and toweis ol the churches. þÿ It was after eleven o'clock, when the procession in front of the Presidential man sion presented a complete line, and a lew minutes before twelve, a funeral car, being a platform raised in the centre, covered with biack velvet, and drawn by six wh.te liorses> a colored man, dressed in while muslin, ac-

cording to the Turkish costume, with a black scait, being at the head of each horse entered the square, and drew up within the portico. In the meantime, the service was performed over the corpse in the east room which was hung with black cambric, in the presence of the A ice 1 resident, the Cabinet, the members of the old Cabinet, the foreign Ministers, the Clergy, and such others as had the privilege of admissiou,

I recisely at twelve o'clock, a detachment of trumpeters, which had been marched up in front of the portico, played the German hymn, during which the body was moved, and placed on the car. 1 he coffin was covered with a rich velvet, on which were placed two swords, laid acioss, and a roll of parchment, with a profusion of fresh hyacinths. At a signal, the artillery iri front of the square sent forth its thunders, the hell of St. John's Church began to toll, and the mourners and others left the mansion, and the procession began its march. Just after it had been put in motion, the Maryland Legislature, which had just reached the depot, where a military escort had been stationed to receive them, marched

up the avenue, and were received into the station in the line which had been 'leserved for them. The length of the whole procession is computed to have been about a mile and a hall ; and the military escort amounted to from one thousand to fifteen hundred men; and a more soldierly exhibition has never been witnessed in the city. The bells of the different churches and lire companies tolled, and the guns at the various stations took up the fire, as ihe procession came up. It was near three o'clock when the gates of the Congress Burying Ground opened to reecive the mournful cortege. There the body was taken from the car, and placed on a bier, which was carried slowly, and with frequent intervals of rest, by a detachment of artillery men> surrounded by a number of pall bearers, to the public vault, where the residue of the service was read, and the corpse was placed in the spot prepared for its reception. The marines then fired several excellent vollies, the guns of the flying artillery pealing forth their thunders in the intervals, and the procession resumed its march homewards. It was the universal impression, so far as I could glean it, that tl,e procession was larger, and the whole effect more imposing, than that of the pageant of the Inauguration. The marines mustered in great strength, and exhibited a truly soldier ly appearance; and the cor| s of U »S. Flying Anillery attracted great admiration. I have never seen any thing to surpass the solemnity of the whole scene.

The Vice President appeared to be much affected, and if a judgment might tie foimed from his countenance, felt the deep responsibility of his new position. Mr. Ewing, the Secretary of the Treasury was, at times, almost unmanned by the excess of his grief. Mr Webster, Air. Bell, Mr Granger, and AD. Crittenden, evinced, by their depoi imeut that they felt their loss. 'Ihe discharge of minute guns continued during the day. We have now laid the venerable chief in bis tomb ; and to morrow, the business of Government, and the hum of lite, w ill he resumed, and the cerenmnh s which have pierced us with such deepsorrow to-day, will gradually fade from memoi \ . and serve only to adorn a page in the history of our country.

The following lines, from an English paper, were written during the pressure of 1825, but are quite as applicable to the pressent period of commercial distress

CONFIDENCE AND CREDIT. The day was dark, the markets dull, The "Change was thin. Gazettes were full, And half the town was breaking ; The counter sign of cask was "stop!" Bankers and Bankrupts shut up shop, And honest hearts were aching.

When near the Bench , my fancy spied A faded form, with hasty stride, Beneath griefs burthen þÿstooping Her name was Credit, and she said, Her father, Trade, was lately dead, Her mother, Commerce, drooping.
The smile that she was Wont to wear Was withered by the hand of care, ller eyes had lost their lustre; Her character was gone, she said, For basely she had been betrayed, And nobody would trust her.
That honest Industry had tried To gain fair Credit for his bride, And found the ladv willing; Bnt ah I a Fortune hunter came, And Speculation was his name, A Rake, not worth a shilling.
The villain was on mischief bent, He gained both Had and Mam's consent And then poor Credit smarted ; He filched her fortune and her fame- He fixed a blot upon her name, And left her broken-hearted.

When thus poor Credit seemed to sigh Her cousin Confidence came by, (lUethiaks he must be clever ;) For when he whispered in her ear, Shtj checked the sigh, she dried the tear, And smiled as sweet as ever.

The Atwress. þÿ We give below ihe firs1 add ress from President Tyler, to the people. The publication of the article, at the present time, is very apt, as much anxiety has existed to know the course he would pursue as Ghief Magistrate. President Tyler's Address lo lite People of the United States. OFFICIAL. To the People of the United States. Fellow Citizens. þÿ Before my arrival at the Seat of Government, the painful communication was made to you by the officers presiding over the several Departments, of the deeply regretted death of William Henuy Harrison, late President of the United States. Upon him you had conferred your suflrages for the first office in your gift, and had selected him as vour chosen instrument to correct and reform all such errors and abuses as had manifested themselves from time to time in the practical operations of the Government- While standing at the threshold of this great work, he has, by the dispensation of an allwise Providence, been removed trom amongst us, and by the provisions of the Constitution, the efforts to be directed to the accomplishing of this vitally important task have devolved upon myself. This same occurrence has subjected the wisdom and sufficiency of our institutions to a new test. For the first time in our history, the person elected to the Vice Presidency of the United Slates, by the happening of a contingency provided for in the Constitution, has had devolved upon him the Presidential office. The spirit of factiont which is directly opposed to

the spirit of a lofty patriotism, may find in this occasion for assaults upon my administration. And in succeeding, under circumstances so sudden and unexpectedly and to responsibilities so gieatly augmented, to the administration of public affairs, I shall place in the intelligence and patriotism of the People my only sure reliance My earnest prayer shall be constantly addressed lo the all-wise and all powerful Being who made me, and bv whose dispensation 1 am called to the high office of President of this Confederacy, understanding to carry out the principles of that Constitution which I have sworn " to protect, preserve, and defend." The usual opportunity which is afforded to a Chief Magistrate upon his induction to office of presenting to his countrymen, an exposition of the policy which would guide his administration, in the form of an Inaugural Address, not having, under the peculiar circumstances which have brought me to the discharge of the high duties of President of the United Stales, been afforded to me, a brief exposition of t ho principles which will govern me in the general course of my administration of public affairs would seem to be due as well to myself as to you. In regard to foreign nations, the groundwork of my policy will be justice on our part to all, submitting to injustice from none. While I shall sedulously cultivate the relations of peace and amity with one and all, it will be my most imperative duty to see that the honor of the country
shall sustain no blemish. With a view to this, the condition of our military defences will become a matter of anxious solicitude. þÿ The Army, which has in other days covered

T3B3!T$3?1E>23X itself with renown, and the Navy, not innp propriately termed the ritrht arm of the public defence, which has spread a light of glory over the American standard in all the waters of the earth, should be rendered replete with efficiency. In view of the fact, well avouched by history, that the tendency of all human institutions is to concentrate powet in the hands of a single man, and that their ultimate downfall has proceeded from this cause, 1 deem it of the most essential importance that a complete separation should take place between the sword and the purse. No matter where or how the public moneys shall be deposited, so long as the President can exert the power of appo ntiiig and removing, at his pleasure, the agents selected for their custody, the Commander-in chief of the Ami and Navy is in fact the Treasurer. A permanent and radical change should therefore lie decreed. '1 he patronage incident to the Piesidcntial office, already great, is constantly increasing. Such increase is destined to keep pace with the growth of our population, until, without a figure of speech, an aitnv of olhceholders niay he spread over the land. The unrestrained power exerted by a selfishly ambitious man, in older either to perpetuate his authority or to hand it over to some favorite as his successor, may lead to the employment of all I tie means within his control to accomplish Ins object I he right to remove from otlice, while subjected to no jusi restraint, is inevitably destined to pro-

duce a spirit of croaching servility with the official corps, which, in older lo uphold the hand which feeds them, would lead to direct an aciive interference in the elections, both State and Fedeial, thereby subjecting the course of State legislation to the dictation of the Chief Executive Officer, and making the will of that officer absolute anu supreme. I will, at a proper time, invoke the action of Congress upon this subject, and shall readily acquiesce in the adoption of all pioper measures which are calculated to attest these evils, so full ol danger hi their tendency. 1 will remove no incumbent from office who has faithfully and honestly acquitted him self ol the duties of his olfiee, except in such cases vvlieie such officer has been guilty of an active partisanship, or bv secret means þÿ the less manly, and therefore the inoie objectionable þÿ lias given his official infiueuce lo the purposes of party, thereby bringing the patronage of the Government iulo conflict with the freedom of elections. Numerous removals may become necessary under tins rule. These will be made by nie through no acerbity of feeling. 1 have no cause to cherish or indulge unkind feelings towaids any, but my conduct will be regulated by a profound sense of what is due to the country and its institutions; nor shall I neglect to apply the same unbending rule to those of my own appointment. Freedom of opinion will be tolerated, the full enjoyment of the right of suffrage will he maintained, as the birth

right of every American citizen, but I say emphatically to the official corps, " thus far and no farther." 1 have dwelt the longer upon this subject, because removals from office are likely often to arise, and would have my countrymen to understand the principle of the Executive actions. In all public expeiiditmcs, the most rigid economy should be resorted to, and. as one of its results, public debt in time of peace be

TT1S% -mi-.jwcLma sedufe '"sly avoided. A wise and patriotic constituency, will never object lo the interposition of necessary burdens for useful ends, and tru e wisdom dictates the resort to such means, in order to sillily the deficiencies in the revenue, rather than In those doubtful expedients, which, ultimatirig in a public debt, serve to embarrass the resources of the country, and to lessen its ability to meet any great emergency which may arise. All sinecures should he abolished. The appropriations should he direct and explicit, so as to have as limited a share of disctetion to the disbursing agents as may >e found compatible with ihe public service. A strict responsibility on the p;i 1 1 of a II their agents of the government, should he maintained & peculation or defalcation visited with immediate expulsion from office, and the most condign punishment. The public interest also demands ihot, if any war has existed between the Government and the currency, it shall cease. Measures of a financial character, now having the sanction of legal enactment, shall he faithfully enforced until repealed by the legislative autlority. But 1 owe it to myself to declare that I regard existing enactments as unwise and impolitic, and in a high degree oppressive. 1 shall promptly give mv sanction to any constitutional measure which, originating in Congrrss. shall have for its object the restoration of a sound circulating medium, so essentially necessary to give confidence in all the tians-

aciiotis of life, Insecure to industry its just and adequate rewaids, and to re-establish the public prospeiitv. Jn deciding upon the adaptation of anv such measure to the vnd proposed, as well as its conformity tr> lie Constitution, I shall resort to ihe Fathers of the great Republican school for advice and instruction, to be drawn from their sage vn ws of our system of Governmu lit, and the light of their ever glorious example. The institutions under which we five, my countrymen, secure each person, in the perfect enjoy ment of all his rights. The spectacle is exhibit' d. to the world of a Govemnu lit deriving its powers fr< m the conse nt of the governed, and having imparted to it otdy so much power as is necessary for its succe ssful operation Those who are charged wiih its administration should carefully at, stain from all attempts to enlarge the range of p owers thus granted to the several de p<ai intents of ihe Government, other than by an apqeal to the people for additional grants, lest by so doing they elisluib that balance whie-fi the patriots and statesmen who framed the Constitution designed to establish between the Fedetal Government and the SStales composing the Union. The observance of these rules is enjoined upion us bv that feeling of reverence and affection which finds a place in the heart of every patrieit, for the preset vation of union and the blessing of union þÿ for the good of our children and our children's childten, through countless generations An opposite eeiurse

could not fail toge-ne tate factions, itiietit upon the gratification of their selfish ends; to give birth to local and sectional jealousies, and to ultimate either in breaking asumier the bonds of union, or in building up a central system, which would inevitably end in a bloody sceptre and an iron crown. In conclusion. I l>eg you to be assured that I shall exert myself to carry the foregoing principles into practice during my administration of the Government, and, confiding in

©/3T3IK; tbe protecting care of an ever watchful ami and overruling Providence, it shall he m v first and highest dutv to preserve unimpaired the free institutions under winch we live, and transmit them to those who shall succeed rne in their full force and vigor. JOHN TYLER. Washington, April 9, 1841.

On Sunday last was dedicated to the service of educating the children of the labor ing peasantry of our Island, the first of the capacious and commodious School houses lately erected, on Great Princess Estate. A highly respectable audience was present ; the services were performed by the Reverend Mr. Breutel, the Moravian Bishop, assisted by all the United Brethren. A most appropriate, judicious, and truly christian discourse was delivered by the Reverend Mr Koemcr in English, who for more than an hour highly gratified his hearers, with sentiments drawn from the only true source, and suitable for the occasion : his text being " Sutler little chil. dren to come unto me for of such is the kingdom of Heaven" No Sectarian views were introduced, nor any thing advanced that could give offence to those of other denominations of Christians The preacher returned thanks to His Mhj. sty the King, to the Governor General, and to the proprietors, for their liberality in erecting and providing for these schools, and drew a lively picture of the great advantages which must result Irom the happy commencement of a system of christian education among the children of the hitherto ignoraut peasantry, and which will draw down the blessings of Heaven Upon those who have been instrumental in effecting tins great change which more than any that has vet taken place will tend to raise from a state of unmerited degradation that portion of our community, laboring under a system whose evils are already greatly mitigated, and which, let

us hope, by the power of that Divine Religion we profess, may, ere long, cease altogether. Several hundred children were present, and bv their decent and cotnely appearance added much to the interest of the occasion.

We cannot conclude without expressing our satisfaction that the task of educating the children has been assigned to tfie Moravian Bret in en, by His Excellency the Governor General, for their primitive simplicity, patience, and peculiar missionary character, fit them better for the task than any others, and their well established usefu'ness and the good effect experienced upon the conduct of the negroes, has been universally acknowledged wherever their missionary establishments have existed. May they reap their reward ! Hymns composed for the occasion were sung, assisted by the Garrison Band witli good effect, and the services concluded greatly to the satisfaction of a crowded auditory,

Letters from St Thomas announce the melancholy intelligence of the sudden decease of the newly electee President of the United States, General Hariison on the 4th A p i 1 at Washington, just one month afier his inauguration. Perhaps no event could have occurred in the Uniieu States, causing such universal regret and mournful feelings, for fie was deservedly popular from the amiabiiiiv, benevolence and the undisput' if integi i \ of tus character. The extracts we this day give from the New York evening paj«r ol l lie 3d instant, render this intelligence hut too authentic It is probable that the great menial excitement and fatigue the President must have undergone, together with the arduous «j tries in succeeding lo an othce full of pre ni difficulties, both with regard to its foreign rein tions and to the embarrassed state of the finances, were the first causes which produced the melancholy catastrophe. The constitution of the United States prescribes that in case of the death of the President, the Vice President shall succeed to his office. It will of course now devolve upon the newly elected Vice President, Governor Tyler of Vnj;iiiia, who for some years was a memocr of the Senate of the U. S. He isconsi lered a very able man, a decided friend to the estaniisiiincut of a National Bank, and opposed to tne whole Jackson and Van Bureri policy. Front the New York Commercial Advertiser April 3, 1841. The Illness of President Harrison It is with deep regret that we have still to announce the continued severe indisposition of the President. We give below all the intelligence received by this morning's mail. þÿ Letters from Philadelphia say that the most intense feeling pervades the community, and adds thai the passengers by the last train of cars from the South bring very unfavorable repirts. From the Express of this morning. Washington, .April. There is great nnxietv if not alarm, respecting the serious illness of General Harrison, which is almost the only and the all engrossing topic of conversation. There has been a consultation of physicians to-day, who broke up at three o'clock, pro nouncing his illness serious, but yet indulging in earnest hopes of his recovery. The disease is stated to be a bilious pleurisy, caused by a severe cold, and constant occupation and excitement Depletion was resorted to yesterday, which has much reduced him, and as he has his mind in as lively exercise as ever, none despair of his recovery, though all areof course, exceedingly anxious. Mr. Webster came back in thenars tonight. Public business is in a great degree suspended by the General's illness. St. Croix Christiansted, Thursday April 29, 1841. Sum': extracts from the St James1 Chronicle of the lfiCi March will be found in our columns. It will be seen that great apprehensions of a war between England and the United States existed in the former country. These have been roused by a hostile report made by Mr. Dickens, Chairman of the Committee of Foreign relations in the late Congress, by the Lockport moh, and by the indictment for murder of .Mac Leod. As regards the first, the British press appear ignorant that the report was not acted upon, but was laid upon the table ; that it was generally censured in the United Stales, and was considered as the last desperate act of an expiring faction, to involve its successors in the Cover anient in difficulties, and that the new Congress, which is convened to meet on the 31 si May, has a decided majority opposed to the inflammatory principles of Mr. Utckens' report. The English also labor under gnat mistakes as to the cause of the arrest of Mac Leod. It was neither an act of" the National or State Governments þÿ It was simply caused by the owners of the Caroline, ( taking advantage of Mc Lead's presence at Lockport, to obtain payment in some way for their loss,) having him arrested, and their making oath before the Grand Jury that he was one of those who burnt her and who committed the murder The Grand Jury were obliged to find the bill against him. It must be remembered, that at that time, the declarations of the British Government, justifying the destruction of the Caroline were not

known in the United States Mac Lend stood in the. place of any other individual criminally charged, and neither the. General nor the State Government had the right to interfere with the proceedings of the Courts ; but now the British Government having assumed the responsibility of the destruction of the Caroline, Mac Lead will probably be set at liberty by the Court. The question of the violation of the territory of the United States by that act, remains to be settled, as well as the capture of American vessels engaged in the lawful African trade by British cruisers, on suspicion only. It will be remembered that alt ho' the American Government have, declared the Slave trade criminal, they have authorized no foreign Government to execute their own laws, These, together with the Boundary questions foim senous subjects to be settled by the new administration. It is to be hoped they are all susceptible of an amicable, adjustment. At the. last dates General Scott of the. United States army had been ordered to assume, the. command of the Niagara frontier, and some, companies of U S. troops had been detached by him, to proceed to Lockport to maintain order Mac Lead's counsel had obtained permission from the court to have his trial removed to another county, if, they thought his safety required it.

Advices from China to the 18 lh December arc received pr: packet. Admiral Elliott had sailed for England in the Volage on account of ill health. The. naval command devolved upon Commodore Sir James Gordon Bremer, who was blockading Canton river with three ships of the line, Jour frigates, four sloops of war and four war steamers. He had threatened to destroy the forts at the Hague, if farther delay on the. pait of the Chinese was made. Mr. Staunton, the English Chaplain, had been given up by them and hud arrived at Macou,

It is said the Chinese, offer five millions of Dollars as indemnity far Bt ilish losses ; but that this was not accepted. The contrary Monsoons having set in, prevented any farther operations against the Northern and Eastern part of China. A most dreadful sickness prevailed at Chusan, so that out of several thousand troops only six. hundred men remained fit tor duty. It is called in England, the Chinese Walcheren.

From the St. James's Chronicle March 16. , We have tins day learnt that our government, in order to piepare for am emergency that may spring out of the case of AJc'l.eod (and if the republic execute him, we do not think there is n man in this United kingdom but will demand justice), have directed six regiments to hold themselves hi readiness to embark for North America þÿ two of which are the 19th and 84th regiments, now to Ireland. It is also stated in private letters from the first circles in Farts, that Land Granville, on the 27th ult , officially announced to M. Guizot that the English government would find it necessary to send 10 sail of the line to the same quarter. Of course a fleet of steamers will form part of such an expedition. þÿ Hampshire Telegraph.

FRANCE. (ntom our private correspondent.) 1'A K FS, March 13 It is stated that the protocol signed in London on the 5th instant, and addressed to the Fiench government, having for its object the final settlement of the Eastern qu . stum, including France as a party, is most likely to terminate in a favorable result This statement comes from veiy creditable quarters indeed. It is also asserted that M. Guizot, so far from looking upon the late news from America as calculated to re awaken other views in the French government, magnanimously disdains taking advantage of any pro bable embarrassments likely to arise Irom the Anglo-American dispute. Indeed, the modelate and perfectly impartial tone adopted by the ministerial journal, the De.btas, in conveying to its readers the accounts received from America, confirms in no small degree the opinion just referred to The Thiers journals assume some credit upon the score of philanthropy in refraining lrom any lively expressions of satisfaction at the prospect of war, injurious alike to England, accused ol having broken the alliance with France, and Ameti ca, whose name is by no means agreeably associated with their historical recollections. It appears that at Havre the sensation unused by the threatened hostilities is very great þÿ The trade between France and the States is carried on principally through that port, and as the supposed first act of the British government in case of war would he to blockade the American ports, the trade of Havre would tie

at once suspended a consideration which lends to cool all sympathy in that quarter. It is not believed here that the differences with America will end in war. In fact, the irregular proceedings of the Americans are such as it is thought cannot be countenanced by any government. The general protest of the w hole English press against the unjust proposition to explain away the hereditary rights conferred upon the Facha of Egypt, by ex eluding Ibrahim, has produced the happiest cfluct upon public opinion here.

THE EASTERN QUESTION. (From the Morning Herald) We have reason to believe that the protocol agreed to by the conference of London for regulating the affairs of the East, and for terminating the Quintuple Treaty of July, uf well as the treaty of Unkiar Skeltsse, has been accepted by the French government. The result to be expected from this circumstance is, that France, Austria, and Prussia, will proceed to a gradual, if not immediate, disarming.

LONDON. þÿ TUESDAY, MARCH 16. The Paris papers confirm the impression generally entertained in this country, that the Great Powers w ill not support the pretensions of the Sultan as conveyed in his recent firmans to Mehemet Alt '1 tie Fresse, asserts that M de St. Auiaire had written to Paris to say that Prince Metternieh was indignant at the course pursued by the Divan, and had declared that the honour of the Four Powers would he compromised if they did not prove that they were no parties to the faithless act of the Forte. The blame of these monstrous conditions appears to be universally attached to Lord Ponsonby. The Paris papers are chiefly occupied with speculations on the result of this new emhrogli.o, and the ticklish state of our relations with America, to w hich country, indeed, thev promise, in the event of hostilities, the best offices of France Our Gallic contemporaries do not, with a single exception, appear to he conscious that a war between America and England would he nearly as injurious to the commerce of France as to that of either of the belligerent Powers. The journalists of M. Thiers, however, blinded, by their fiatred to England, to the rousequenres to France of a war between this country and the United States, regard it only as a contingency which will a fiord to France an opportunity of assuming that position among the nations from which the treaty of July had led her to exclude herself. Marshal Soult has followed up his reprimand to officers of the army for writing in newspapers by an order prohibiting the read-

ing of newspapers or political tracts in the different barraeks of France, not without exciting the most hitter comments on the despotism of such a measure from the Libera! and Gvcu Royalist journalists

OPINIONS OF Til K FRENCH I'KESS ON THE AMERICAN (QUESTION. The Cowrier Francois, one of the best informed and most reasonable of the Liberal papers contains an article on t he subject, from which we take the following extract; þÿ " We hope on the eve of a struggle which would cause a great effusion of blood, and which presents no chance of compensation for the calamities of war. the two governments will giveaway to reflection, and feel some remorse lor I tic passions winch have led to the present danger. I' ranee, indeed, has no reason to lie alHicted at the prospect of a war between England and the United States, for such a war might tie for us, so far as a selfish policy is concerned, a source of jov and triumph ; but we must he above the paltry suggestions of private interest. Viewing the question on a larger basis, such a war would interrupt the commercial relations which connect the two continents, and which during the last 25 years have reached a vast extension. In this point of view, I fie war would he a calamity for Europe War sometimes promotes the cause of civilisation. Thus the English could have rendered vast services in India, if they had ameliorated the condition ol the people whom tliev subjected. So, in conquering Algeria, we shall sooner or later have the power of doing good to the uncivilised tribes with whom we are now contending ISut on what principle can a war between the English and the Vmcricans be beneficial ? The Loudon Journals announce i lie intention of stiring up

the slaves of the southern states to revolt; aod. on the other hand, the citizens of New Y ok and the VI nine have probably the intention of sliring up revolt amongst the oppressed French colonies in Canada On boih sides, then social war would he added to foreign war. and the contest would be carried on at the same time by scaffolds and by can non. What an example for the civilised woild! If vvar should lake place between these two nations, it will not he a war ol principle, for there is no question of right involved; it will he a conflict prompted by ambition and fed by pride ; that is to say, the most odious spectacle that could be ollered by human nature We will not inquire which of the two countries could do most harm to the other. They are both powerful, and botli pi'fs<'vering, and obstinate in their designs. þÿ England has an incontestable superiority at th s moment, and her first blows would be strong ones With II ships of the line, 15 frigates, and ,'1'J smaller vessels of war, the United Stales would hnd it difficult to contend against the most formidable navy of the tti'i verse; but they have sailors and a warlike population, and money will not be wanted for the building of ships. England has been unfortunate hitherto in her wars with the United Stales, and her government may desire to take signal vengeance for the past. The reminiscences ol the past, on the contrary. raise the pride of the Americans, and they hope this time to take possession Canada, of

and to drive the English from their comment. This is the chapter of illusions of both coun tries the reality will be terrible. If war should take place, it will lull upon the two nations as a judgment from Heaven upon their reciprocal insolence, and the Satanic pride which led to it. The United Slates will thus expiate their ingratitude to France, which made them what they are, and England will pav the penalty of her disloyal intervention in the East." The CunstitiitiiiTinrl is more violent, and lets out the whole of the rancour ot its party against England : þÿ " /Is tar as we can judge from the information communicated in the journals and letters from the United States, it is not a party, but the entire country, which has expressed its inflexible determination to put down the pretensions ot England The real question with the Americans is not as to whether Mc'Leod shall or shall not be hanged, or whether their territory shall lie enlarged by a few hundred leagues which are contested: these nrc the reasons assigned, and not the cause of rupture. What the Americans desire is to dohver themselves for ever from the presence of

2>AlT33£ TST'ITTDTS the English in Canada, and to fiee the new northern would from the patronage of Euiope; and for this they have waim auxiliaiies amongst ihe Canadians themselves, who have, by so many acts of bold resistance and so ntany sacrifices, shown their Uislike ol the yoke which is imposed upon them In this respect, then, the war which appcats to be at hand will in the United States, be a national one, and no government can, on this point, modify the general feeling of the country, or even hesitate to follow the general impulsion. The rights of i lie executive are vet \ limited, ton limited, perhaps, by the constitution. þÿ The nation has delegates, hut in reality it governs by itself. What p demands its agents must execute, and the shades of political opinion which distinguish the two great parties, and which are very slight, have no importance as to the solution of a question upon which public opinion and .the represen tatives of the states and of the federal union have pronounced their will unanimously." In this violent course the Constitutional is followed by its apt fellow labourer in the harvest of mischief, the SSutional ; þÿ ' We hope the United States will be firm and resolute to the end It will not be the first time that they have lowered the British pride, which lias always increased in insolence with thi: humility of his adversaries þÿ Eet the Americans hear their own history in mind ; they will find in it just grounds for confidence, and the whole world will be in debted to them if they succeed in shaking a

power, whose immoderate ambition is the source of annoyance and anxiety both to old and new states." These absurdities are balanced by a few quiet words in the Gazelle de frt ttnee, which in our opinion embrace the whole question : þÿ " The consequences ol such an event, says the Gazelle, would be immense for us All our commercial interests are engaged in our relations with America. Our silks, our wines, our jewellery, our furniture, our articles of fashion and luxury from a large capital ; all this would he placed in jeopardy, for the first act of the English would be to blockade the ports of the union."

From the New York Commercial Advertiser, March 27, 1811. From the Montreal Herald. W c are not apprehensive of a war, because the American government is perfectly aware that it is weak to a proverb in warlike preparations and defences, and that the nation is virtually bankrupt in resources, without a character good enough to borrow money from foreign countries, and least ol all, from England. That there will be a good deal of buz-fuz and attempt at bullying we do no! doubt, hut after all, Mr. Mc Leod V'i" quicklv given up, and the disputed territories of New Brunswick, and Columbia river, will be handed over to Great Ibitam very amicably while the national vanity of the Americans will be tickled by an assurance that as they neither wish to impose nor be imposed upon, thev have sacrificed their feelings to a sense of justice; or, to use the language of one of their Presidents, who said that "the sober second thought of the people was always right, never wrong." We onlv put this on record now. that it itnv be seen bv and live how very little of a prophet is the Montreal Herald. W ith the most sincere desire for peace w ith England þÿ and with all the rest of the world too þÿ and w ith an earnest hope that the boundary question, and the Ale Leod question, and all other questions, will vet he harmoniously disposed of, we /oust take leave to say that if no other result is contemplated, or will be admitted by England, than that which the Herald speaks of, that haimooious adjustment is impossible. The American people are not averse to
making concessions þÿ hut those concessions must be reasonable, and be mutual.

From the Philadelphia (iaxette. Steam Frigate' Mississippi' þÿ We have had much gratification an/1 pride in examining the splendid national steam frigate now being built at the navy yard, and in viewing its powerful and efficient machinery in pro gress at the works of Messrs. Merrick and Towne. ll such formidable defences he mul- j Gen. S. that

be brought to aid the undisputed skill of our national marine, a bulwark of defence mav j and abide he presented to anv hostile movement of transatlantic powers which will enable us to laugh them to scorn The vessel to which we now refer will be an armed steam frigate of the first class Her dimensions on the water line are þÿ length 218 feet, breadth 4'i feet, giving a sectional horizontal area of 8720 square leet. Her depth is 23 j feet. Her mean immersion 18| feet and her tonnage may he stated at a little under '2000 tons. The cylinders of her engines aie each 75 inches diameter and 5 feet stroke. Her paddle wheels 30 feet diameter. 8be will lie supplied with four copper boilers constructed in the most efficient manner, with stowage for 800 tons of coal. Her boilers will expose about 1 0,(100 square feet of heating surface to the action of ihe furnaces, which, with coals of average goodness, would he sufficient to produce an efficient working power of 1000 horses. But the engines will be worked greatly under this power, the expansive principle being applied to an almost unlimited exterit. Mechanical expedients are provided in the machinery by which the steam may he cut off at any repaired part of the stroke.

The adoption of copper boilers renders less necessary the use of brine pumps or any of the other contrivances which have lately been introduced in seagoing steamers, for keeping the water in the boiler from being salted. The copper takes no incrustation, and the loose deposit may always he dismissed by the blow-off cocks which are provided in these boilers. Indeed, with proper attention on the part of the engineers, no deposit should ever lie allowed to he formed. The boilers should always lie blown off before the solution in them reaches the point of saturation, and to secure this desirable result we would recommend the use of the hydrometer guages lately introduced with much advantage in English steamships bv Messrs Seaward. The paddle wheels will be the divided split paddle, generally used in American vessels. Without the expensiveness and mechanical complexity of shilling or feathering paddles' this form of wheel possesses most _ot their practical advantages, and none of their practical inconveniences. The valves bv which the steam is admitted to, and withdrawn from the cylinder, are cylindrical metallic valves, which act without packing, and appear to us to be preferable to the I) slide, generally used in European marine engines. The hoiiers are tested to a pressure of 30 lbs per square inch above the aunospheie, and intended to be worked at a pressure not exceeding 15 lbs. The vessel will be rigged and fitted out as a frigate, and armed with ten guns, two ten inch long guns, and 8 42 pounders.
We should observe that the boilers and great steam passages will be coated with felt, to save the heat otherwise lost bv radiation.

isthmus is about thirty miles þÿ but by pursuing the course of the river Chagres to the town of Cruces, some twenty five miles from its mouth, ships can go within fifteen miles of the Pacific þÿ ami at this place the Franco Grunadian Company will commence operations. THE THEFT. Young love descended onee from Heaver), Upon a soft and balmy gale, As the last tints of rosy even Their lustre pour'd o'er hill and vale. þÿ
And in the twilight, pure and tender,. Bright shone his pinions' varied plumes, With all the hues of changeful splendour The neck of Juno's bird assumes.
But ah ! a cruel poet, straying, Whose bosom love had long heguil'd, Beheld htm "mid the roses playing, And seized the unsuspecting child. þÿ
And (while the deed the muse rehearses, Her eye a tear of sadness (ills) þÿ He pluek'd it. to pt n his amorous verses, From Cupid's pinions all the quills.
Long time the bov god wept distress'd, 'Till woman saw his deep despair ; She clasp'd him to her gentle breast, And bade him soothe his sorrows there.
And nestling there, beneath her eyes, it seeinM so like his home above, tie ail forgot his native skies, And fell no more a wish to rove.
And since that hour, in woman's heart, His purest dwelling Love has made ; While still his plumes to song impart The sweetness of their tuneful aid.
Then shoidd'st thou ever doubt again The power of song the soul to move, Remember that the poet's pen W as stolen from the wing of Love. Dublin University Magazine.

New Orleans, Feb. 23, 1841. James Watson Webb, Esrq. Dear Sir þÿ I he news of the suspension of the Philadelphia Banks has had the effect to cause very extensive operations in the cotton market. & upwards of 20,000 bales have been taken within the last two davs, at an advance fully of t of a cent, and holders seem disposed to advance the rates daily. We flfow quote from ordinary to fancy at from 9 to 14c ; the concurrent opinion here is that the crop will Dot exceed 15 or 16.000 bales, at the extreme figure, and as our English buyers are now basing their purchases upon this calculation, and are sending to England information to this effect, we may expect to see cotton, before the season closes, attain as high a rate here as it did in the spring of 1839 þÿ or rather the Nolle spring. The crop of Sugars will also fall short upwards ot 40,000 hhds and many Planters who made last year 700 hhds. now this season make but 280 hhds and the probability is that next year we shall make no Sugar at ail, as tiie severe and protracted rains have prevented the planting of the cane. There is no good Molasses now to be had on the coast> and it is selling readily on the Levee at 23c. cash We shall probably not make a quarter crop of good Molasses, there will be a largo quantity o| sour Molasses sent north, as the Planters have ground up their frozen cane into molasses. In fact, the whole of the production of the sunny and sweet South will be very materially þÿshort so I advise you to lay

in a supply of sugar, cotton and molasses, for family use. Provisions are horribly low, ar.d no markets at any price. Our Levee is groaning under the weight of those great staples of the west, pork, lard, beef, bacon, <&c. &c., piled upon it mountains high, waiting for a more benign change in the state of things. Exchange on New York, at sight 4 a 5 per cent.; Philadelphia, no sales; United States notes 12 per cent, discount. Yesterday we celebrated the birth day of Washington, with gnuid Pe Di.um, and the pomp of military parade, and the day being March Gras, the closing of Lent. We have a grand carnival in the streets ; already masks and characters of the most grotesque and nondescript kind are passing my þÿwindows some in wheelbarrows, same in carts, some in gorgeous carriages with eight horses, some on donkier riding þÿbackwards and should one of our quiet descendants of the Pilgrims, drop in upon us on this day, he would think he was in a country where the people had taken leave of their þÿsenses and he would not be much mistaken. I shall be happy to give you a line from þÿ these parts" once and a while, if agreeable to you. ! remain, truly yours. Remark þÿ Our þÿcorrespondent s favors will always be acceptable to us and valuable to our readers, as no gentleman in New Orleans is better qualified to give us facts in regard to the crops and motley þÿmarket. Ed. Cour, Enq.

Philadelphia, March þÿC 5 P. M. We have had but little of interest stirring. The movements of the Legislature of our State are so tardy that we are yet without any enactment by that body by which to re. gulate the monetary affairs of our community.

Bairns TKmroasa aagsaaaima The Money and Stock market continue in a state of much depression, without any assignable cause, except the apprehension of disastrous news from England, caused by the intelligence w hich will have reached there of the failure of the attempt of the Pennsylvania Banks to continue specie payments, and of the singular report made bv Mr. Pickins in the House of Representatives, on the subject of the relations of this country wirti England. þÿ The effect of the fatter, we should think, must be greatly counteracted by the almost general disapprobation with which this document was received here; it certainly will have been subsequently, when the debate in the Senate on the same subject reached there, and we hesitate nothing in asserting that from every appearance, there is no danger of an interruption to the existing harmony in the relations between the two countries. As to the Pennsylvania suspension, though really an untoward event, we cannot see that it makes matters intrinsically any worse than before the attempt was made. We have no apprehension of the return of any drafts drawn by or on account of the United States Bank, having reason to believe these were predicated on arrangements definitely concluded and based on the securities of the States, which, though under a temporary depression, no one believes will not prove eventually good in rhe full extent of the word. The Money Market is rather pressed þÿ Auctioner, som afholdes The Banks are particular in the selection of

paper, and 10 a 12 per cent, discount is asked in the street, though from the stagnation in business there is not much paper offering. The market for merchandize are very inactive ; there does not appear to be life or activity in any one article.

EXPRESS FROM MARSEILLES. By an extraordinary express, in aniicipation of the overland mail, we have received despatches from China, India, and all parts of the East. Our dates are from Chusan to the 20th of December, from Macao to the 27th of January, from Singapore to the 25th of January, from Calcutta to the 18th of February, from Madras to the 20th of February, from Sciade to the 22d of February, from Bombay to the 1st of March, and from Alexandria to the 25 th of March. The steamer Enterprise had arrived at Calcutta from Macao on the 14th of February bringing despatches for the Home Authorities, which were forwarded to Bombay by express, and thence transmitted to Suez by the Victoria steamer. It appears, that in consequence of the insincerity and tardiness displayed bv the imperial Commissioner preparations were made on the morning of tire 9th of January for attacking the outposts of the Bogue forts. About 7U0 Sepoys, 200 European soldiers, and 400 seamen and ma rines were embarked under the command of Major Pratt, of Iter þÿMajesty gOih s Regiment, in the steamers Enterprise, Nemesis, and Mad agascar. and landed in the vicinity of the fort of Chuenpee. At the same time her Majesty's ships Calliope, Larne, and //jacinth opened a cannonade on the lower battery of the fort, while the steamers Nemesis and Queen threw shells into the upper tower which commanded it The latter was soon taken possession of by the British troops, who poured down a heavy lire of musketry on all

the lower works, and quickly drove the Chinese from their guns. In two hours the fort was iu the possession of the English, with a loss of only 3 killed and 23 wounded ; that of the Chinese is estimated at from 500 to 700. Many were killed in the attempt to escape by jumping down from their embrazures, a depth of 20 feet to the rocks below. The ships and crews escaped unhurt, although the fort mounted 35 guns. At the same time the fort of Tekoktow was attacked by another squadron operating about 3 miles to the southward, under command of Captain Herbert, of the Samarang, supported by the Ib uid. Modeste, and Columbine. A heavy fire was opened on the fort, and promptly returned, but the Chinese guns were speedily disabled, and a party of seamen landed to seize the fort. The Chinese made a spirited resistance, hut were soon overpowered, and the fort captured. The first lieutenant of the Samarang was wounded in the assault. The steam vessels then attacked the fleet ! of junks lying in Anson's Bay, but owing to : British the shallowness of the water, only the Nemesis could approach them, towing 12 armed I boats from her þÿMajesty s hips. Her first rocket set fire to the powder magazine of one junk ; 18 others were blown up by their own

Doctor Lund who at present resides in Lagoa Santa in Brazil, had informed the society that he in a lately finished journey into the interior of Brazil, had for the first time found human bones in a cave along with bones of

decidedly extinct animals, which must be of an extraordinary great age, probably the oldest human bones hitherto discovered, as they in part are completely petrified, and in tfieir state of preservation entirely similar with those of the extinct animals, in connexion with which they are found. They will theiefore throw a light on the condition of the inhabitants in this part of South America in times, which go far behind our historical acquaintance with this part of the world The construction of the forepart of the head is remarkable, as the forehead does not rise in the same plane as the face but forms a considerable angle therewith, whereby it differs from the cranium of all human beings at present existing This proportion becomes so much the more remarkable, as the human figures which are found drawn or engraved on the old Mexican mon uments also represent a race of men, who so to say entirely want the forehead and therefore have something remarkably brutal thereby In connexion with these remarkable bones a semicircular formed stone was found quite smoothed on the lower side which evidently has been used to rub with. The following paragraphs, which we copy j from the London Morning Chronicle, are deserving of notice, as showing the opinions are current in relation to the prospects of peace in Europe. There are now the greatest hopes and fullest prospect of a good understanding between France and England. We must own that from the very first we thought the alliance insecure, when we saw French zeal, in imaginary possession of Egypt, pushing for the conquest of Syria, and getting þÿ to use their own expression on horseback, in the Red þÿ Sea, between us and India. THE LEVANT MAIL. The Otloman fleet, after remaining a few days at St. Stephano, waiting a favourable wind, set sail on the 16th, and shortly afterwards entered the Bosphorus. The Sultan had repaired in his steamer to the Kiosks of the Seraglio Bournon in order to witness the event. The Mahmoudieli ship of the line took the lead, and on doubling the point of the Seraglio fired a salute of 21 guns, which his i highness ordered should be instantly returned i All the other vessels of the fleet followed the example of the Mahmondieh. The fleet consisted of 26 sail ; eight ships of the line, ten frigates, two corvettes, and six brigs, and other light vessels. The entire population of Constantinople and its environs lined the banks of the channel, and crowned the heights which overlook the city, in order to enjoy the spectacle. It was computed that only 3.000 of the crews of the fleet had returned to Constantinople. In June, 1839, when it left for Alexandria, they amounted to at least 21,000 men. The res! had died o the plague or remained in the service of Mehemet Ali. All the vessels were in the most filthy condition. Letters from Alexandria represent the Pasha as sulky, and the armaments and recruiting as active.

In the ahsensg of Mr. Fox, detained bv indisposition, the Russian Minister, Mr. Bodisco, appeared at their head : þÿ As the members of the Body were respectively presented, the President spoke to each of them of the relations, present or past, between bis country and the United States, and of bis hope of the continuance of amicable relations ; and received from all congratulations, and the assurance of the desire of peace ami amity with Ins country.
